Final project proposal

Yitian(Ethan) Chen

2026-11-18

Source: vignettes/proposal.qmd

To: BST260 Teaching Team, Fall 2026

1. Background

I plan to study BMI and blood pressure in NHANES and compare foodborne and waterborne outbreak sizes in CDC data. These questions let me practice the data cleaning, visualization, and regression methods covered in BST260. They also involve different units of analysis: participant records and reported outbreaks. I will analyze the datasets separately.

2. Research questions

  1. NHANES: Among adults aged 40–79 in the 2011–2012 NHANES teaching data, how is BMI associated with average systolic blood pressure after accounting for age, sex, and race/ethnicity?
  2. CDC outbreaks: Among reported single-state outbreaks in the 50 states and Washington, DC, during 2009–2019, how does the number of illnesses per outbreak differ between foodborne and waterborne outbreaks after accounting for year and region?

3. Data sources and study populations

NHANES

I will use NHANES::NHANES from version 2.1.4 of the NHANES R package. The original source is the National Center for Health Statistics’ NHANES survey. The package manual describes this as a 10,000-row teaching dataset resampled from NHANESraw. Repeated IDs are expected, so I will keep them. One row is a resampled participant record.

I will select the 2011–2012 cycle and ages 40–79. Age 80 is top-coded, so I will leave that group out rather than treat 80 as an exact age. I will use the package’s teaching approximation for the analysis. Population estimates would require the original survey files and sampling design.

CDC outbreaks

I will use waterborne, supplied in the course template. Its original source is the CDC National Outbreak Reporting System (NORS data and dictionary). The template records the API endpoint as https://data.cdc.gov/api/v3/views/5xkq-dg7x/query.json. I will keep the bundled data/waterborne.rda from template commit 0f4c7076c5b572aaacef22ba49f18dbfee7883da, accessed November 20, 2026. The original extraction date is not recorded.

The dataset includes several transmission modes despite its name. I will select Food and Water records from 2009–2019, a period available for both modes and before COVID-19. The main analysis will include single-state outbreaks in the 50 states and DC. I will count excluded multistate, territory, and missing-location records separately. One row represents a reported outbreak.

4. Variables and missing data

NHANES

Role Variable and coding
Exposure BMI, continuous in kg/m²; use BMI / 5 so the coefficient refers to a 5-unit increase.
Outcome BPSysAve, continuous average systolic blood pressure in mmHg.
Adjustment Age in years, Sex as a factor with female as reference, and Race1 as a factor with White as reference. All recorded race/ethnicity categories will be retained.

Age and sex are related to blood pressure and body composition. Race/ethnicity may reflect differences in social conditions and access to care. These background considerations motivate the adjustment set, although it will not remove all confounding. I will not interpret race/ethnicity coefficients as biological effects. The NHLBI overview provides background on blood pressure risk factors.

I will report missing values for each analysis variable and use complete cases for the models. Missing BMI, blood pressure, or adjustment variables will remain NA. I will record how many rows are excluded and compare available characteristics of included and excluded records.

CDC outbreaks

The exposure is primary_mode, with Food as the reference and Water as the comparison. Other or missing modes will be excluded. The outcome is illnesses, a numeric count of reported illnesses per outbreak. It is not a population infection rate.

I will adjust for year as a factor and for the four regions in datasets::state.region, assigning DC to the South. Reporting practices and outbreak types may vary across years and regions, which is why I chose these adjustment variables.

I will turn the list into a table, check numeric fields, and preserve absent fields as NA. I will report missing and nonpositive illness counts. Those records cannot enter the log-size model, and records missing an adjustment variable will also be excluded from that model.

5. Planned analysis

NHANES

I will check variable types and ranges, then report the mean, SD, median, IQR, and range for continuous variables and counts and percentages for categorical variables. A scatterplot with a fitted line and a smooth curve will help me check the shape of the BMI–blood pressure relationship.

Using the same complete-case sample, I will fit an unadjusted linear model and then BPSysAve ~ I(BMI / 5) + Age + Sex + Race1. The main result will be the estimated difference in mean systolic blood pressure per 5-unit increase in BMI, with a 95% confidence interval. I will check residual plots, a Q–Q plot, and influential observations. As an exploratory analysis, I will add a BMI-by-sex interaction to see whether the slope differs by sex.

CDC outbreaks

I will tabulate outbreak counts by mode, year, region, and month. For outbreak size, I will report the median, IQR, mean, and range. A boxplot on a log scale will help compare the distributions when some outbreaks are much larger than others. Monthly plots will use year and month as an index, not an exact onset date.

I will fit log(illnesses) ~ primary_mode + factor(year) + region. Exponentiating the Water coefficient gives an adjusted geometric-mean ratio, which I will report with a 95% confidence interval. It does not give a ratio of arithmetic means or an individual’s infection risk. I will check residuals and influential records. Large outbreaks will stay in the main analysis; as a sensitivity check, I will refit after excluding counts above the pooled 99th percentile. If the model fits poorly, I will explain the problem and give more weight to the descriptive results.

6. Limitations

NHANES provides a cross-sectional association, so the analysis cannot show what would happen if a person changed their BMI. Blood pressure medication, diet, activity, and other unmeasured factors may affect the association. Missing data and the resampling used to create the teaching dataset also limit interpretation.

NORS only includes outbreaks that were detected and reported. Illness counts may be incomplete, and the pathogens and settings may differ between Food and Water. Adjustment for year and region will not remove all these differences. I will describe patterns in reported outbreaks without claiming that one mode causes larger outbreaks. The CDC dashboard FAQ describes further reporting limitations.

7. Project organization

After feedback on this proposal, I will prepare two analysis vignettes, one for each dataset. Each will include the data source, cleaning steps, descriptive tables and plots, methods, findings, and limitations. I will use executable R code, write reusable functions for repeated tasks, record package versions, and set a seed if I use simulation. The reports will be published on this R package’s pkgdown website through GitHub Pages.

AI assistance

For this project, I chose to study BMI and blood pressure in NHANES and compare foodborne and waterborne outbreak sizes. I approved the proposed analyses and used ChatGPT/Codex for help with the unfinished coding and technical setup. It also helped explain the methods, check results, and draft and revise the proposal.
